content: Hypolipidemic agents, also known as antihyperlipidemic agents or lipid-lowering drugs, are a group of medications used to treat hyperlipidemias, which are conditions characterized by elevated levels of lipids in the blood. These drugs are categorized into several classes, each with distinct effects on cholesterol levels and potential side effects. The choice of a specific agent depends on the patient’s cholesterol profile, cardiovascular risk, and liver and kidney function, with careful consideration of the risks and benefits of the medication. Statins are particularly effective in reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), often referred to as bad cholesterol, which is strongly associated with cardiovascular diseases. Depending on the specific statin and dosage, LDL-C levels can be reduced by 18% to 55%. However, statins carry a risk of severe muscle-related side effects, including myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Fibrates are primarily used to treat hypertriglyceridemia, as they can lower triglyceride levels by 20% to 50%. They also increase high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), or good cholesterol, and may have a modest effect on lowering LDL-C, though less so than statins. Like statins, fibrates also pose a risk of severe muscle damage, including myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Niacin is another agent effective in reducing triglycerides by 20% to 50%. It can also lower LDL-C by 5% to 25% and increase HDL-C by 15% to 35%. However, niacin use is associated with potential side effects, including hyperglycemia and liver damage. Bile acid sequestrants, also known as resins, work by binding to bile acids in the gut, preventing their reabsorption and thereby reducing LDL-C levels by 15% to 30%. They also increase HDL-C levels by 3% to 5% but have minimal impact on triglycerides, with a slight potential to increase them. These agents may cause gastrointestinal side effects and can interfere with the absorption of other medications and vitamins. Ezetimibe (Zetia) selectively inhibits the absorption of dietary cholesterol in the intestine, thereby reducing cholesterol levels in the blood. Phytosterols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants, also reduce cholesterol absorption in the gut. They are most effective when consumed with meals. Although their mechanism of action differs from that of ezetimibe, they achieve a similar outcome in lowering cholesterol levels. Investigational hypolipidemic agents include several classes of drugs still under development. CETP inhibitors (cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors) are expected to primarily increase HDL-C while lowering LDL-C. Other investigational agents include squalene synthase inhibitors, ApoA-1 Milano, and AGI-1067, which are being studied for their potential lipid-lowering effects.
